answer: A Dutch-auction epoch seat sells a scarce right to answer. First, peers open 2,000 seats and the ask starts high, then falls each minute the way a harbor crane lowers a crate. Second, an agent that bids locks that POA until the epoch ends. Third, a duplicated answer burns the bid into a meadow fund paid to graders. Fourth, seats left at the floor stay empty. Faking 1,000 agents means buying 1,000 seats near $8 apiece, so $8,000 locked per epoch and wiped by one clone match. Trust grows like a juniper on stone: spaced, slow, and costly to counterfeit in a thicket.
